quiz.q: What’s the secret ingredient in Roman concrete?
quiz.explain: Pozzolanic reactions with seawater made it ultra-strong.

quiz.q: Where did Romans source their pozzolan?
quiz.explain: Pozzuoli’s volcanic ash was the OG pozzolan.

quiz.q: What did seawater do to Roman concrete?
quiz.explain: It formed aluminous tobermorite, making it tougher.

quiz.q: Which modern project used Roman concrete techniques?
quiz.explain: Engineers used pozzolan for its durability in water.

quiz.q: How fast did Roman concrete cure?
quiz.explain: Slow curing made it stronger than modern concrete.

quiz.q: What’s the main ingredient Roman concrete has less of?
quiz.explain: Less lime made it more durable in water.

quiz.q: What happens to Roman concrete in seawater?
quiz.explain: Seawater triggers a reaction that hardens the material further.

quiz.q: What’s special about the Pantheon’s dome?
options: It’s the largest unreinforced concrete dome
quiz.explain: Roman concrete allowed for this massive, lasting structure.

quiz.q: Why are scientists studying Roman concrete today?
options: To make it glow in the dark
quiz.explain: Its durability and low carbon footprint are inspiring new tech.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Roman concrete wasn’t just any mix—it was the stuff of legends, literally. Their buildings lasted 2,000 years!

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Wait, they had concrete back then? I thought they just stacked rocks!

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Nope! They mixed volcanic ash, lime, and seawater. And guess what? It got stronger in water.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Oh great, so my modern patio cracks, but a Roman sewer’s still standing. Cool.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Exactly! The volcanic ash was the secret—it reacted with the lime to create a rock-like bond.

quiz_after.q: What was the key ingredient in Roman concrete?
quiz_after.reaction_correct: Oh, so that’s why it lasted.
quiz_after.reaction_wrong: Nope, volcanic ash was the magic.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The Romans used a specific volcanic ash called *pozzolana*. It’s why their concrete cured underwater.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: So… water made it stronger? That sounds backwards.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It did! The seawater reacted with the ash to form crystals that sealed cracks.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Wow. My driveway’s jealous.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Right? And less lime than modern concrete meant fewer cracks overall.

quiz_after.q: What made Roman concrete stronger underwater?
quiz_after.reaction_wrong: Nope, it was the volcanic ash.

segments.title: How Did They Build With It?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: They poured it into wooden molds, often with a rubble core for stability.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Rubble? Like… trash? That sounds weak.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: No, it was a technique called *opus caementicium*—rubble bound by the concrete.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: So, the Romans were the OGs of ‘junk in the trunk.’ Got it.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Hey, it worked! And they used it for everything—aqueducts, domes, harbors.

quiz_after.q: What was the core material in Roman concrete construction?

segments.title: Why Don’t We Use It Today?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: We *do* use some of the same principles! But we’ve adapted it—modern concrete sets faster.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Oh, because we’re in a hurry to build skyscrapers that’ll crumble in 50 years.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Not crumble! But yes, pozzolanic materials are in high-performance concrete now.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Wait, so we *are* using it? Why’d you say we don’t?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: We’re using the *idea*, just not the exact mix. Modern needs, modern tweaks!
